### G1 — the shipped GEMM's schedule (2026-09-29)

Filed as **§6.5** in `research/6.5-gemm-schedule.md`.

**The loop, from the disassembly** (`dit_gemm_wg128x256_bt16_swz8`,
wave64, 240 VGPRs, no spill, no LDS; ACO says 6 subgroups a SIMD, which
is not the arithmetic of a 1536-register file at wave64 and is not
relied on). One iteration is one 16-wide K tile:

| instructions | count | what |
|---|---|---|
| `v_wmma_f32_16x16x16_f16` | 32 | the 4×8 accumulator grid |
| `buffer_load_b128` | 24 | 4 A + 8 B fragments, 2 loads each, in 3 clauses |
| `s_add/s_mul/s_lshr/s_lshl/s_load/s_mov` | 56 | the B tile addresses, **recomputed every iteration** |
| `v_lshlrev/v_add3/v_mul_lo/v_mbcnt/v_and` | 29 | the A addresses and lane offset, likewise |
| `s_delay_alu` | 20 | dependency stalls in that arithmetic |
| `s_waitcnt` | 9 | `vmcnt(14)`, then 12, 10, … 0, four MMAs between each |
| `s_clause`, branch, compare | 5 | |

Order: address arithmetic → all 24 loads → `s_waitcnt vmcnt(14)` (A and
the first B landed) → 4 MMAs → wait → 4 MMAs … → `vmcnt(0)` → the last 4
→ loop. **G-o3 answered: no.** ACO does not hoist the next tile's loads
above this tile's MMAs; each iteration pays the load latency once, from
the address arithmetic to the tenth load landing, with only the other
waves on the SIMD to fill it. 4.5 non-MMA instructions an MMA, so it is
not issue-bound by count (H3); but ~85 of them sit on the critical path
in front of the loads.

**Occupancy does not move it** (`-DLDS_PAD`, an unused shared array that
caps workgroups a WGP; `H3_GEMM_SPV`, 480p, int8):

| build | LDS | workgroups a CU | gemm qkv | gate / up | o | forward |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| shipped | 0 | ≥ 3 | 36.9 | 36.6 / 36.6 | 34.5 | 30.10 s |
| `LDS_PAD=4096` | 16 KB | 4 | 37.2 | 36.7 / 36.6 | 34.1 | 30.21 s |
| `LDS_PAD=8192` | 32 KB | 2 | 37.3 | 36.6 / 36.5 | 34.2 | 30.04 s |
| `LDS_PAD=16384` | 64 KB | **1** | 37.6 | 37.0 / 36.9 | 34.7 | 30.00 s |

Flat to 1%, down to one 4-wave workgroup a CU. So the exposed latency is
not being covered by other waves at *any* of these occupancies, and
adding waves is not a lever (G-o2 is moot for this kernel).

**Take the memory system away** (`-DL0_LOADS=1`: every fragment load
reads one of two K tiles, so the 24 loads are issued and waited for as
before but every one is an L0 hit; the result is garbage by
construction; the `down` projection keeps the shipped KRANGE build, so
it is a control):

| | shipped, real loads | `L0_LOADS` | |
|---|---|---|---|
| gemm qkv | 36.9 | **43.6** | 1.18x |
| gemm gate / up | 36.6 / 36.6 | **44.2 / 44.0** | 1.21x |
| gemm o | 34.5 | **42.8** | 1.24x |
| gemm down (control, real loads) | 26.7 | 29.9 | the clock |
| attention (unchanged kernel) | 37.2 | 39.4 | the clock |
| sclk during the forward | 2600–2650 | 2650–2700 (less memory power) | |
| **per clock, FLOP/clk/CU** | **353 (74%)** | **~405 (82–85%)** | |

So the gap decomposes: **~10 points are the memory system** (the
difference between L0 hits and the real slabs, at the same schedule),
and **~16 points are the in-wave schedule** with the loads perfect: the
once-a-tile stall from the address arithmetic through the L0 latency to
the tenth load, against ~1,090 clocks of MMA. Neither part responds to
occupancy, which is what the LDS arms say.

**What G2 builds, in order** (re-ranked by the energy roofline, §0.7).
(1) Strength-reduce the addresses: every fragment's offset advances by a
constant per iteration, so the 85 instructions are 12 adds; cheap,
bit-identical, shortens the critical path in front of every iteration's
loads, and issue costs watts (the 4-chain probe burns 14 W more than the
16-chain one for the same MMAs). (2) Fewer bytes a FLOP: LDS sharing of
each slab across the workgroup's 4 waves (the two waves that share an A
slab each load it today; H6, untested at this tiling) and the largest
per-wave tile the registers allow, measured in TFLOP/s *and* W, because
traffic is the power and the power is the clock. (3) Prefetch one K
tile ahead into a second register set, so the loads a wave waits on
were issued 1,090 clocks earlier: +24 VGPRs, which at WN = 8 means a 4×4
or 8×4 grid instead; it buys the in-wave stall and no clock. Bit-identical
C for all three, `TestGPUForward`; every arm reports GFLOP/J.

**Hypotheses after G0/G1:** H1 confirmed and larger than thought (10%
of the ceiling is the clock; G7 asks whether anything can be done about
it). H2 alive as the in-wave stall, not as an occupancy story. H3 alive
only as the address arithmetic on the critical path. H4, H5 unmeasured.
H6 is the ~10 memory points. H7 dead.

### G2 — the prefetch that fits (2026-09-29)

Filed as **§2.9** in `research/2.9-lds-staged-wave32-gemm.md`, with the
whole ladder. The shipped build is now `dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32` (and
`_krange`): eight wave32 waves of 4×4 tiles in the same 128×256
workgroup, the K slab (two tiles) fetched by the workgroup as 6 `uvec4`
a lane a slab ahead, written to the other of two LDS planes behind the
MMAs, one barrier a slab, fragments read from LDS at a conflict-free
pitch of 36 halves. Bit-identical to the wave64 build (`H3_GEMM_REF`,
`TestGPUForward`).

| 480p, int8 | qkv | gate / up | o | down | forward | sclk | per clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| wave64 4×8 (was shipped) | 37.2 | 37.3 / 37.1 | 35.4 | 28.7 | 29.86 s | 2620 | 74% |
| **`lds_w32`, two runs** | **41.1 / 40.9** | **40.7 / 40.7** | **38.9 / 39.1** | **40.8 / 40.6** | **27.16 / 27.11 s** | 2665 | **80%** |

The three findings that decided it: **a wave64 fragment is 8 VGPRs**
(4x replicated across the lane groups), so §6.5's "+24 VGPRs" for a
prefetched tile was +96 and no register prefetch fits beside a 4×8
grid; **ACO copies a fragment carried across a loop back-edge element
by element** (200 `v_mov_b16` a trip), so the two register-pipelining
arms were dead before they ran, and only a build that carries nothing
(a hoisted two-tile slab: +18% at the same intensity; or LDS) measures
the idea; and **wave32 and LDS are one lever**: wave32 halves the bytes a
fragment read moves but caps the tile at 4×4 and, fed from global memory,
runs at 21.5; fed from LDS it runs at 40.9. Refused on the way, all
bit-identical: strength-reduced addresses (nothing: the arithmetic was
never the cost), four hoisted tiles (no better than two), the read
order inside a slab (nothing), LDS pitches of 16 and 24 halves (the
reads are `ds_load_b64`, 16 lanes a clock: 4-way and 2-way conflicted).

**What is left** (§2.9 item 5): with the staging loads all L0 hits the
build reaches 82% per clock, so the global side is ~3 points and the
LDS-side schedule (64 `ds_load_b64`, 6 stores, a barrier and the
`lgkmcnt` ladder a 544-clock slab) is ~18. G-o8.

### G8 — the carry-in (2026-09-29)

Every host of the 128×256 kernel now creates `dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32`
pinned to wave32 (a `wave` field on each variant table; `K % 32` where a
host checks its tiles), through its own gate and screen, the same
session, the machine otherwise idle:

| host | gate | screen, old → new | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `h3/dit` | `TestGPUForward`, bit-identical | 480p forward 29.86 → 27.11 s | G2 |
| `h3/vae` | `TestGPUDecoder`, PSNR 81.7 dB unchanged | 480p decode 37.1 → **35.5 s** device, 768p 66.1 s | its bias column made K = H + 16; K now rounds to the big GEMM's tile (`gemmVariants[gemmBig].bk`), the pad columns zero in A and B |
| `qimage/dit` | `TestGPUOracle1024` | `TestGPUGEMMScreen`, one staging: swz8 2179 → **`lds_w32` 2058 ms a step** (−5.6%; swz2/4/16 +30/+18/+10%) | the fifth arm of the screen, the default |
| `ace/dit` | `TestGPUDiT` | 8 forwards at 30 s / 2 / 4 / 10 min: **wave64 0.96** / lds 3.27 (w64 3.24) / **6.76** (6.93) / **18.79** (19.37) s | **the LDS build loses at 375 rows** (130 against 120 ms: 30 workgroups, the barrier shows), ties at 1500, wins 2.5–3% from 3000; `bigW64Rows = 1024` picks the wave64 build below that; the 64×64 rung is 131 / 488 / 1002 / 3215 ms, never the answer |
| `kev` (fp16 bank) | `TestGPURowMatchesKev` | `TestGPUGEMMLadder`, 494 tokens: 154.2 → **132.4 ms** (reg64 at 37 tokens 49.7 both days, so the machine is the same) | serves int8 (`q8m4`, 155.3 at 494), which the fp16 rung now beats there: G5's argument |
| `parakeet` | `TestGPUEncoderStack` | ladder, `wg128x256`: 138 / 384 / 768 / 1024 frames 28.8 / 36.9 / 67.3 / 111.6 → 31.1 / 40.9 / 66.9 / 109.1 ms | its plan never picks the rung (`reg32x32_w32` wins every clip); at 8–12 workgroups the build loses 8–11% |
| `zimage/qwen` | `TestGPUEncoder`, `TestGPUKernelsAgree` | — (its rung is the >192-token one) | rung name now `wg128x256_lds_w32` |
| `ocr` | `TestLM`, `TestEngine` (all six cases token-identical) | the page's 1,234-row prefill 100 → 102 ms | the prefill is 2.5% of a page |
| `ace/lm` | `TestLogits`, `TestDeterministic` | prefill 239 rows 106 ms | rows ≤ 256 are GEMVs |

**The rule it adds:** the LDS-staged build needs the machine full. Its
per-slab barrier and staging cost show whenever the grid is under ~40
workgroups (rows × N / 32,768), and the hosts whose inputs are short
(parakeet, the LM prefills, a 30 s clip) already run smaller rungs or a
wave64 build there. Where a host's screen gave a number, it is above.

## How to run

- The suite: `go run ./cmd/bench -h`; families `peak`, `gemm_wmma`,
  `shapes`, `stride`, `moe`, `bank`. Results append to `results/*.csv`

  (§0.2).
- The ISA: `RADV_DEBUG=shaderstats go run ./cmd/probe shaders/X.spv [32|64]`
  and `RADV_DEBUG=asm …` (`MESA_SHADER_CACHE_DISABLE=1` for a repeat).
  Builds are `go generate ./shaders` lines in `shaders/shaders.go`; `.spv`
  is gitignored.
- A GEMM build from disk through H3: `H3_GEMM_SPV=path` (`H3_GEMM_WAVE=32`

## Open questions

- **G-o8.** The LDS-side schedule is the remaining ~18 points of

<!-- §2.9 — KERNELS.md G2. The section number is the stable identifier
     cited from shaders/, bench/, cmd/, vk/ and the root docs. Do not
     renumber it. -->

[← IDEAS.md](ideas.md) · [research index](README.md) · the fp16 GEMM's schedule

### 2.9 The prefetch that fits: K slabs staged through LDS at wave32 — **done** ✅ (2026-09-29)

**Question** (KERNELS.md G2, after §6.5): the shipped fp16 GEMM
(`dit_gemm_wg128x256_bt16_swz8`, four wave64 waves of 4×8 accumulator
tiles, one K tile a slab) pays one exposed load latency a K tile and
runs at 74% of the ceiling at its clock; with every load an L0 hit it
reaches 82–85%. Can the next tile's loads be issued before this tile's
MMAs, bit-identically, inside the register file?

**Answer: not as fragments, as a slab.** The shipped build is now
`dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32`: eight wave32 waves of 4×4 tiles in the
same 128×256 workgroup, the K slab (two 16-wide tiles) fetched by the
workgroup as 6 `uvec4` a lane into 24 staging registers, in flight for
the whole of the previous slab's MMAs, written to the other of two LDS
planes behind them, one barrier a slab, and the fragments read from LDS
just ahead of their MMAs. Same MMAs in the same order per accumulator,
so **bit-identical** (`TestGPUShapes`'s `H3_GEMM_REF` gate against the
wave64 build's velocities; `TestGPUForward`).

**480p H3 forward** (`H3_SHAPES=480 H3_PROFILE=1 H3_BANK=q8`, the
machine otherwise idle, 100 ms clock and package-power samples; per clock
is FLOP/clk/CU against the probe's 480):

| build | qkv | gate / up | o | down (KRANGE) | forward | sclk | per clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| shipped wave64 4×8, one tile | 37.2 | 37.3 / 37.1 | 35.4 | 28.7 | 29.86 s | 2620 | 355, **74%** |
| **`lds_w32`** (+ its KRANGE companion) | **41.1 / 40.9** | **40.7 / 40.7** | **38.9 / 39.1** | **40.8 / 40.6** | **27.16 / 27.11 s** | 2665 | 385, **80%** |

Two runs of the winner agree to 0.2%. The down projection, whose 235 MB
A chunk overflows the MALL and which M11d could only take from 26 to
29, is at the other projections' rate: the workgroup reads its A slab
once instead of once a wave. All at 154 W, the package cap.

**How it was found: the ladder, every rung bit-identical, in order.**

| arm | build | qkv | per clock | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SR`: strength-reduced addresses (§6.5's 85 instructions a tile → 12 scalar adds + 12 lane folds) | wave64 4×8 | 37.2 | 74% | **nothing**: the address arithmetic was never the cost |
| `PIPE`: A0/A1 double-buffered in the 16 spare VGPRs, A2/A3 and every B reloaded in place after their last MMA | wave64 4×8, 252 VGPRs | 34.3 | 68% | **dead on this compiler**: ACO cannot coalesce a loop-carried cooperative-matrix fragment; every one crosses the back-edge as ~16 `v_mov_b16` (200 + 134 moves a two-tile trip) |
| `DB`: a full second fragment set, the next tile issued before this tile's MMAs | wave64 4×4, 8 waves | 36.7 | 73% | the same moves (128 + 66); not a measurement of the idea |
| the AI-32 control: 4×4, one tile, no prefetch | wave64, 8 waves | 32.6 | 64% | the intensity drop from 43 to 32 costs 13% |
| `k2`: 4×4, two-tile hoisted slab (`BK_TILES=2 HOIST_A=1`), no carried fragments | wave64, 8 waves, 192 VGPRs | 38.4 | 77% | +18% over its control at the same intensity: the prefetch works when the compiler is not asked to carry it |
| `k4`: four tiles hoisted | wave64, 256 VGPRs | 37.2 | 72% | no better than two |
| `LDS_STAGE` at wave64 4×8, pitches 24 / 16 halves | 256 VGPRs, 36 / 28 KB | 31.0 / 25.5 | 58% / 47% | the fragment reads come out as four `ds_load_b64`, for which the LDS serves 16 lanes a clock, and a 12-dword pitch is 2-way conflicted; pitch 16 is 4-way |
| `LDS_STAGE` at wave64 4×8, pitch 36 | 256 VGPRs, 54 KB | 36.5 | 70% | conflict-free, still under the shipped build |
| **`LDS_STAGE` at wave32 4×4, pitch 36, one tile a slab** | 8 waves, 240 VGPRs | **40.7** | **78%** | |
| **… two tiles a slab** | 256 VGPRs, 54 KB | **40.9**, o 39.4 | **79%** | **shipped** |
| the wave32 control: 4×4, direct loads, no LDS | 192 VGPRs | 21.5 | 40% | wave32 alone is a disaster: a tile is 272 clocks of MMA and the latency is the same |
| `STAGE_L0`: the staging loads all L0 hits (wrong by construction) | | 44.0 | 82% | **the global side is now ~3 points**; the rest is the LDS-side schedule |
| `LOAD_ORDER`: reads issued A0, B0..B3, A1.. so the first MMA waits for the 2nd fragment, not the 5th | | 40.6 | 79% | nothing |

**What it says.**

1. **A wave64 fragment is 8 VGPRs, not 2.** The hardware holds an A or
   B operand four times over (lanes 16–31, 32–47 and 48–63 replicate
   0–15; `coopmat_layout_probe.comp`), so a prefetched *fragment* costs
   4x its bytes in registers and 4x its bytes on the L0-to-VGPR path,
   which is why §6.5's "+24 VGPRs" was +96 and why no register-resident
   prefetch fits beside a 4×8 accumulator grid. At wave32 the replication
   is 2x. A prefetched *slab* costs each byte once, in 24 staging
   registers.
2. **ACO will not carry a fragment across a loop back-edge.** Both
   register-prefetch arms compiled to hundreds of sub-dword moves a
   trip (a coopmat is a vector of 16-bit elements, and a phi it cannot
   coalesce is copied element by element). Any cross-iteration register
   pipelining of cooperative-matrix operands is dead on Mesa 26.2.2, and
   a build that carries none (a hoisted multi-tile slab, or LDS) is the
   only shape that measures the idea. `PIPE` and `DB` stay in
   `dit_gemm.comp` as the record of that, never built.
3. **LDS reads of a cooperative matrix are `ds_load_b64`**, whatever the
   alignment, so the conflict-free pitch is 18 dwords (36 halves) apart
   between the 16 lanes of a fragment, not the 12 (24 halves) that a
   128-bit read would want. §2.1's LDS arms had no pad at all (a pitch
   of 8 dwords, 4-way conflicted) and an [N, K] B gather; that is why
   they lost by 1.2x in 2026-09-14, and it was not the mechanism.
4. **Wave32 and the LDS are one lever, not two.** Wave32 halves the
   bytes every fragment read moves and doubles the accumulator's
   registers, so its largest tile is 4×4 (AI 32) and, fed from global

Three compiler/hardware facts about cooperative matrices on this part (Mesa 26.2.2 RADV, RDNA3.5), established in KERNELS.md G2 / research §2.9 (2026-09-29):

- A 16x16 fp16 A or B fragment is **8 VGPRs at wave64 and at wave32** (the hardware replicates it across the 16-lane groups: 4x at wave64, 2x at wave32), and a fragment load moves 4x (2x) its 512 B through L0→VGPR. The accumulator is 4 VGPRs at wave64, 8 at wave32.
- **ACO cannot coalesce a coopmat carried across a loop back-edge**: it copies it as ~16 `v_mov_b16`. Any register double-buffering / software pipelining of fragments across K tiles compiles to hundreds of moves a trip and loses. Only shapes that carry nothing (a hoisted multi-tile slab, or LDS staging) measure a prefetch.
- `coopMatLoad` from `shared` lowers to four `ds_load_b64` per fragment, for which the LDS serves 16 lanes a clock: the conflict-free row/column pitch is 36 halves (18 dwords), not 24 (16-lane 2-way) and not 16 (4-way).

**Why:** §6.5 planned a "+24 VGPR" register prefetch that was really +96 and then un-coalescable; two arms were dead before they ran. The shipped GEMM (`dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32`) is LDS-staged slabs at wave32 because of exactly these three facts.

**2026-09-21.** A four-arm 48-layer depth sweep lost three of its four arms.
The script called `go run ./cmd/llm` once per arm; arm 1 had already built and
ran fine; while it ran I edited `shaders/shaders.go` to add a new `//go:embed`
for a `.spv` that did not exist yet, and arms 2-4 each died instantly with

    shaders/shaders.go:2646:12: pattern llm_attn_expand.spv: no matching files found

~25 minutes of measurement, and the failure was silent in the sweep's own log
until the end.

[[strix-halo-bench-runs]] already says "edit *text* while it runs, nothing
else" — that rule is about CPU contention perturbing the numbers. This is a
second, harder reason: **a multi-arm script that invokes `go run` rebuilds the
tree at the start of every arm**, so the source it compiles is whatever the
tree holds *then*, not what it held at launch. Even an edit that compiles
would silently measure a different binary in later arms, which is worse than
a crash.

**How to apply:** make the benchmark script `go build -o <scratchpad>/bench
./cmd/llm` **once at the top** and run that binary for every arm. Then the
tree is free to edit while it runs, and every arm is provably the same build.
Select arms with environment variables read at dispatch time (this is what
`LLM_ATTN_SPLITS` and `LLM_ATTN_CELL_SPLITS` are for), never by rebuilding.

**2026-09-29, the same trap one level down.** A backgrounded swizzle sweep
ran `<scratchpad>/dit.test` once per arm; I then `go test -c -o` the *same
path* for the next experiment and launched it. Two GPU runs overlapped (each
timing the other's contention) and the old loop's later arms ran the new
binary. A shell `until grep -c ...` waiter hid it: the arms I waited on were
not the ones I thought. **Give every sweep its own binary name** (e.g.
`dit_swz.test`), and before starting a GPU run, check `ps` for another
`*.test` / `cmd/*` still on the device, or wait on the sweep's PID
([[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]]).

~25 minutes of measurement, and the failure was silent in the sweep's own log
until the end.

[[strix-halo-bench-runs]] already says "edit *text* while it runs, nothing
else" — that rule is about CPU contention perturbing the numbers. This is a
second, harder reason: **a multi-arm script that invokes `go run` rebuilds the
tree at the start of every arm**, so the source it compiles is whatever the
tree holds *then*, not what it held at launch. Even an edit that compiles
would silently measure a different binary in later arms, which is worse than
a crash.

**How to apply:** make the benchmark script `go build -o <scratchpad>/bench
./cmd/llm` **once at the top** and run that binary for every arm. Then the
tree is free to edit while it runs, and every arm is provably the same build.
Select arms with environment variables read at dispatch time (this is what
`LLM_ATTN_SPLITS` and `LLM_ATTN_CELL_SPLITS` are for), never by rebuilding.

**2026-09-29, the same trap one level down.** A backgrounded swizzle sweep
ran `<scratchpad>/dit.test` once per arm; I then `go test -c -o` the *same
path* for the next experiment and launched it. Two GPU runs overlapped (each
timing the other's contention) and the old loop's later arms ran the new
binary. A shell `until grep -c ...` waiter hid it: the arms I waited on were
not the ones I thought. **Give every sweep its own binary name** (e.g.
`dit_swz.test`), and before starting a GPU run, check `ps` for another
`*.test` / `cmd/*` still on the device, or wait on the sweep's PID
([[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]]).

258	// it element by element (200 v_mov_b16 a trip for PIPE, 128 for DB), which
259	// costs more than the latency they hide: 34.3 and 36.7 TFLOP/s against the
260	// shipped 37.2. Kept as the record, so the idea is re-tried on a new
261	// compiler and not on this one. What did fit is LDS_STAGE, below.

263	// Both read [kStart, kEnd) in tiles; at the last tile the "next" loads
264	// re-read the current one (in bounds, and their results are never used).

266	#define PIPE 0

278	// LDS_STAGE (KERNELS.md G2, research §2.9; the shipped build at wave32, 4x4
279	// tiles, eight waves, two tiles a slab): the K slab staged through LDS, double-buffered,
280	// so the prefetch depth is a whole tile at the 4x8 tile's intensity without
281	// a second fragment set in registers. A wave64 fragment is 8 VGPRs because
282	// the hardware holds it four times over (lanes 16-31, 32-47 and 48-63
283	// replicate 0-15), so a prefetched *fragment* costs 4x its bytes in
284	// registers and 4x its bytes on the L0-to-VGPR path; a prefetched *slab*
285	// costs each byte once: 128x16 of A and 256x16 of B are 12 KB, 3 uvec4
286	// loads a lane, 12 VGPRs, in flight for the whole of the previous tile's
287	// MMAs and written to the other LDS plane behind them. The fragments are
288	// then read from LDS just ahead of their MMAs, off a path that is not the
289	// L0's. One barrier a tile. §2.1 measured LDS staging as a loss on an
290	// unpadded slab (4-way bank conflicts on every fragment read: 16 lanes at a
291	// pitch of 8 dwords) and an [N, K] B gather; here both pitches are
292	// A_LPITCH and B_LPITCH halves, 12 dwords, conflict-free for the 8 lanes
293	// a ds_read_b128 serves a clock, and B is staged as the fragment tiles it
294	// already is. (Measured: the lowering emits ds_load_b64, 16 lanes a clock,
295	// for which 12 dwords is 2-way conflicted; 36 halves, 18 dwords, is the
296	// conflict-free pitch, and it is what ships. Wave32 halves the bytes a
297	// fragment read moves and is the other half of the win: at wave64 the same
298	// build is 36.5 TFLOP/s, at wave32 40.9, the wave64 shipped kernel 37.2.) Same MMAs in the same order: bit-identical. Plain A, tiled B,
299	// one K tile a slab, fp32 C.
300	#if LDS_STAGE && (A_CONV || L0_LOADS || B_LAYOUT != 2 || BK_TILES > 2 || HOIST_A || C_F16 || C_PACK || PIPE || DB)

341	// ds_store_b128 (gemm_wmma.comp verified it in the disassembly).
342	#define SPREAD8(arr, base, v) {                                                \
343	    f16vec2 h0 = unpackFloat2x16((v).x);                                       \
344	    f16vec2 h1 = unpackFloat2x16((v).y);                                       \
345	    f16vec2 h2 = unpackFloat2x16((v).z);                                       \
346	    f16vec2 h3 = unpackFloat2x16((v).w);                                       \
347	    arr[(base) + 0u] = h0.x; arr[(base) + 1u] = h0.y;                          \
348	    arr[(base) + 2u] = h1.x; arr[(base) + 3u] = h1.y;                          \
349	    arr[(base) + 4u] = h2.x; arr[(base) + 5u] = h2.y;                          \
350	    arr[(base) + 6u] = h3.x; arr[(base) + 7u] = h3.y;                          \

363	    coopMatLoad(dst, hact, pc.inOff + (wm0 + (i) * TILE) * pc.lda                  \

371	    coopMatLoad(dst, hact, pc.inOff + (wm0 + (i) * TILE) * pc.lda                  \

396	#define LOAD_FRAG_A(dst, i, k0, kt)                                            \
397	    coopMatLoad(dst, hact, pc.inOff + (wm0 + (i) * TILE) * pc.lda + (k0) + (kt) * TILE, \

402	#endif

415	    coopMatLoad(dst, w16, bAt[j] + (kt) * TILE * pc.ldb, pc.ldb, gl_CooperativeMatrixLayoutRowMajor);

417	#define B_STEP (BK_TILES * TILE * TILE)
418	#define LOAD_FRAG_B(dst, j, k0, kt)                                            \
419	    coopMatLoad(dst, w16, bAt[j] + (kt) * (TILE * TILE), TILE, gl_CooperativeMatrixLayoutColumnMajor);

430	    coopMatLoad(dst, w16, pc.bOff +                                            \
431	        (((wn0 + (j) * TILE) / TILE) * (pc.gemmK / TILE) + (((k0) & 16u) / TILE)) * (TILE * TILE), \

443	// One K-slab: WM A-fragments and WN B-fragments per K-tile, then WM*WN MMAs
444	// against them. With HOIST_A the slab's A loads all issue before the first
445	// MMA, so the wave has BK_TILES*32 bytes of each A row outstanding at once
446	// instead of 32 (§5.1b mechanism 3, §2.7).
447	#if HOIST_A
448	#define MMA_BLOCK(k0) {                                                        \
449	    FRAG_A_T fragA[BK_TILES][WM];                                              \
450	    [[unroll]] for (uint kt = 0u; kt < BK_TILES; kt++) {                       \
451	        [[unroll]] for (uint i = 0u; i < WM; i++) { LOAD_FRAG_A(fragA[kt][i], i, k0, kt) } \
452	    }                                                                          \
453	    [[unroll]] for (uint kt = 0u; kt < BK_TILES; kt++) {                       \
454	        FRAG_B_T fragB[WN];                                                    \
455	        [[unroll]] for (uint j = 0u; j < WN; j++) { LOAD_FRAG_B(fragB[j], j, k0, kt) } \
456	        [[unroll]] for (uint i = 0u; i < WM; i++) {                            \
457	            [[unroll]] for (uint j = 0u; j < WN; j++) {                        \
458	                acc[i][j] = coopMatMulAdd(fragA[kt][i], fragB[j], acc[i][j]);  \
459	            }                                                                  \
460	        }                                                                      \
461	    }                                                                          \
462	}
463	#elif LOAD_ORDER
464	// The reads issued A0, B0..BWN-1, A1..: the first MMA (A0 x B0) waits for
465	// the second fragment to land instead of the (WM+1)th, and each A after
466	// that enables a row of MMAs as it arrives.
467	#define MMA_BLOCK(k0) {                                                        \
468	    [[unroll]] for (uint kt = 0u; kt < BK_TILES; kt++) {                       \
469	        FRAG_A_T fragA[WM];                                                    \
470	        FRAG_B_T fragB[WN];                                                    \
471	        LOAD_FRAG_A(fragA[0], 0, k0, kt)                                       \
472	        [[unroll]] for (uint j = 0u; j < WN; j++) { LOAD_FRAG_B(fragB[j], j, k0, kt) } \
473	        [[unroll]] for (uint i = 1u; i < WM; i++) { LOAD_FRAG_A(fragA[i], i, k0, kt) } \
474	        [[unroll]] for (uint i = 0u; i < WM; i++) {                            \
475	            [[unroll]] for (uint j = 0u; j < WN; j++) {                        \
476	                acc[i][j] = coopMatMulAdd(fragA[i], fragB[j], acc[i][j]);      \
477	            }                                                                  \
478	        }                                                                      \
479	    }                                                                          \
480	}
481	#else
482	#define MMA_BLOCK(k0) {                                                        \
483	    [[unroll]] for (uint kt = 0u; kt < BK_TILES; kt++) {                       \
484	        FRAG_A_T fragA[WM];                                                    \
485	        FRAG_B_T fragB[WN];                                                    \
486	        [[unroll]] for (uint i = 0u; i < WM; i++) { LOAD_FRAG_A(fragA[i], i, k0, kt) } \
487	        [[unroll]] for (uint j = 0u; j < WN; j++) { LOAD_FRAG_B(fragB[j], j, k0, kt) } \
488	        [[unroll]] for (uint i = 0u; i < WM; i++) {                            \
489	            [[unroll]] for (uint j = 0u; j < WN; j++) {                        \
490	                acc[i][j] = coopMatMulAdd(fragA[i], fragB[j], acc[i][j]);      \
491	            }                                                                  \
492	        }                                                                      \
493	    }                                                                          \
494	}
495	#endif

#endif

#define KT_LOOP 0

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

D18: the uniform 4.5-bit plan with `ple_proj` back on int8, 0.0165 GB a token for 0.367 points (4.1850, +3.87%, against the uniform plan's 4.2010, +4.27%), with the bank equal to the simulation to four decimals and the same standard error.** The decode cost is **below the instrument's floor**: three interleaved A/B pairs give means 35.74 against 35.79 with the sign flipping pair to pair, against a within-arm spread of 0.31 tok/s where the bytes predict 0.12 — one pair alone would have read −0.06, another +0.14. **The decision turned out to be three-way per family, not two**: `bank_q4.go:144` is nibbles by construction, so `q5_k` is a kernel stage (a third `qh` stream through the unpack) while int8 is free (a family left off the plan stages on L8a's bank). **The fifth bit recovers 66-77% of a family's whole 4.5-bit cost for a quarter of int8's bytes** — `full_attn` **4.1560 (+3.15%), 14.1 pp/GB**, `lm_head` 4.1743 at 8.0 (and it recovers 77% because unsloth's matrix has **no row for `output.weight`**, so the family is round-to-nearest), `ple_proj` 4.1919 at 47.8 for a 0.196 pp prize — where the *marginal* step from `q5_k` to int8 on `full_attn` is **1.9 pp/GB**, the clearest "stop here" on the frontier. **Idea 4 is closed with both its options losing**: `full_attn` at int8 measures **+2.72%** against the +2.07% additivity predicted, and is strictly dominated by L8c-3's `hc + attn` at `q5_k` (+2.70% at 4.419 GB against +2.72% at 4.592). **Additivity leaks both ways and both leaks are the n-gram block** — `ple_proj` marginal is 0.367 pp where standalone it is 0.59 (P2's 0.22 pp, from the other side), and `hc + attn` recovers 1.54 where the parts give ~1.39 — so **a plan is measured, never composed**. LLM2's ~12 pp/GB for `ple_proj` was quoted *from halves* where every other family was quoted from int8; on the consistent basis it is ~35. **A second corpus (Go stdlib, 145 chunks) leaves the ranking invariant at 2.5x smaller magnitudes** (1.6288 → 1.6560 uniform → 1.6506 D18 → 1.6450 `full_attn` q5_k), with `ple_proj` a *larger* share of the damage on code (20% against 8.7%) and the fifth bit recovering 41% against 26% — so **+3.87% is a wikitext figure and the pessimistic end**. Fresh inventory **4.281 GB a token, 56.5 tok/s ceiling** (arithmetic — not P1's identically-numbered *measured* 4.281). `cmd/serve -llm` stages D18 by default; `cmd/llm` deliberately does not |
132:| [P1a](p1a-hyper-connection-shape.md) | **The hyper-connection block's 485 dispatches: the weightless half fused away bit-exactly, and the other half is a grid rather than a kernel.** The scatter that closes one mixer and the grouped RMSNorm that opens the next are the same 2560 values per (token, stream) written and read straight back, and both were already one workgroup per (token, stream) — so `llm_hc_cn.comp` does both in one pass over registers. **1501 dispatches a pass to 1407, 30.69 ms to 30.37, decode 32.59 -> 32.93 tok/s**, both arms on one build (`LLM_HC_NOFUSE=1` is the control), **prefill 1070.8 -> 1089.2 at ubatch 2048** (an 84 MB read a boundary) and nothing at 512 (21 MB fits the MALL), and **identical to the last place** on `res`, `xn` and `mixed`. The ulp that had to be chased first is worth knowing: the SPIR-V of the two arms is the same `OpFMul`+`OpFAdd`, but giving the sum a **second reader** lets ACO contract it into an FMA, which rounds once where the scatter rounds twice — one ulp on 23% of the residual, and `precise` is the only thing that says no. Then the ruler: the down projection's decode rungs read **the same 1.94 MB off the same bank with a grid that varies twenty-fold**, and **168 workgroups is 9.26 us where 672 is 5.54** — so `up_m1`'s 10.87 us at **160 workgroups and 11.5 KB a workgroup** is not MODE 1's M=1 waste, it is `down_gemv8`'s number at `down_gemv8`'s width. What pins `up` at 160 is the collapse: `packUpB` makes a 64-column block 16 features x 4 streams, so `BN` cannot be 16. A 4x4 block would be 640 workgroups and is **priced at 2.3 us a mixer, 0.22 ms a token, +0.24 tok/s** — not taken, because it is every rung's epilogue on the prefill path |
137:| [L8c-3](l8c-asymmetric.md) | **D7 reversed: at identical bits *and identical bytes* the asymmetric form is 2.06x cheaper, and it is the form calibration works on at all. The 2x2 over the whole corpus, from 4.0289: symmetric 4.6127 rtn / 4.6588 imatrix, asymmetric 4.3124 rtn / **4.1998** imatrix — so calibration is worth −2.80 points on one form and +1.14 on the other.** L8c-2 closed the calibration question with a caveat it could not test: every rung it measured was Q4_0's *symmetric* form, where the checkpoint's own experts — and unsloth's matrix's own target — are Q4_K. **The bytes turn out not to be a trade**: ggml nests the min, a super-block of eight groups of 32 carrying one fp16 pair plus 12 bits a group, which is 0.500 bits a weight — *exactly* what a symmetric fp16 scale per 32 costs — so `q4_k/32` and `q4_0/32` are both 4.500 and every comparison is free of a width argument. Uncalibrated, asymmetric is **2.06x** cheaper end to end (+7.04% against +14.49%) and **3.2x** on the hyper-connection block that decides the plan, against a reconstruction gap of 1.22-1.30x and L0d's claimed 1.043-1.053x — the proxy under-read it twice over. **The larger half is the imatrix**: symmetric it costs more on top of round-to-nearest, asymmetric it *buys* 2.80 points, and it now helps every family it covers (`hyper_conn` +9.04% → **+0.90%**, `deltanet` +1.48% → **−0.30%**). **The mechanism is the second parameter, measured**: a symmetric group has one free parameter and it *is* the gain, so a calibrated fit can only express its preference by shrinking the group — the extra shrinkage calibration costs `hc_attn_up` is **1.24 pp symmetric and 0.47 pp asymmetric**, and on `attn_qkv` it is gone. So L8c-2's rule gains a clause: an imatrix helps in proportion to how evenly importance is spread inside a scale group **and how many parameters that group has to express a preference with**. The port is bit-identical to `ggml_quantize_chunk` over 204 800 values per arm and in **f32**, not merely in the half. One departure from ggml: K-quants want `k % 256 == 0` and `hc_*_up` is 320 wide — the one family the question is about — so its super-block is the whole row, ten groups, 4.475 bits. **D3 comes back and the kernel becomes the next thing to build**: 4.264 GB a token and a **56.7 tok/s** ceiling at +4.24%, or 4.419 and 54.8 at **+2.70%**, both dominating L8c-1's 4.575 / 52.9 / +5.98% on *both* axes |

The routing is the discrete half and the 4 k dump is the only place it can be checked: **0 of 40 960 slots differ as a set** on all 4096 tokens, and the two slots that differ in *order* are a pair the reference's own probabilities put **4.35e-07 apart relative** — so the test demands that any order disagreement be an unresolvable tie rather than demanding the order agree. <!-- §2.10 — KERNELS.md G-o8. The section number is the stable identifier
     cited from shaders/, bench/, cmd/, vk/ and the root docs. Do not
     renumber it. -->

[← IDEAS.md](ideas.md) · [research index](README.md) · the LDS-staged GEMM's remaining points

### 2.10 Every VALU instruction costs the matrix pipe a clock: the LDS-staged GEMM's second K tile as a loop — **done** ✅ (2026-09-29)

**Question** (KERNELS.md G-o8, after §2.9): the shipped LDS-staged wave32
GEMM (`dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32`) runs at 80% of the ceiling at its
clock, and with the staging loads all L0 hits at 82%, so the ~18 points
left are on the LDS side of the kernel: 64 `ds_load_b64`, 6 stores, a
barrier and a `lgkmcnt` ladder a slab. Which of those is it?

**Answer: mostly none of them.** The largest single cost was ~40
`v_swap_b32`/`v_mov_b32` a K tile that the register allocator emits to
assemble the slab's *second* tile's fragments, because the scheduler had
hoisted the next slab's six staging loads above this slab's MMAs and the
second tile's `ds_load`s then landed in whatever pairs were free. On this
part **a VALU instruction costs the matrix pipe about one clock** (the
WMMA runs on the SIMD's VALU; there is no separate tensor unit to
overlap with), so those moves were ~7% of the pipe. Keeping the slab's
two K tiles as a loop the compiler may not unroll (`KT_LOOP`), with the
staging views declared writable so NIR does not sink the staging loads to
their use (`STAGE_RW`), takes the moves out: **same MMAs in the same
order, bit-identical**, H3's projections **40.4 → 43.5 TFLOP/s**, the
split down projection 40.3 → 42.2, a 480p forward **27.30 → 26.71 s**,
**80 → 85% per clock**. Shipped as the same build name, so all nine
hosts of the kernel (§2.9's G8 table) get it with no host change.

**The instrument: a probe that adds the kernel's parts back one at a
time.** `shaders/wmma_issue_probe.comp` is the register-only WMMA loop of
`alu_peak.comp` in the GEMM's own geometry (eight wave32 waves of 4×4
tiles, 55 KB of LDS planes at pitch 36), run through `cmd/bench peak` by
the new `PEAK_SPV` hook (`bench/ops_peak.go`), against the same 480
FLOP/clk/CU:

| added to the register-only loop | FLOP/clk/CU | of 480 |
|---|---|---|
| nothing (`wmma_issue_reg`) | 480–491 | 100% |
| 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 independent fp32 FMAs a lane per MMA | 449 / 422 / 382 / 318 | 93.5 / 88 / 80 / 66% |
| a workgroup barrier every 16 MMAs | 480 | 100% |
| the A fragments re-read from LDS each tile (4 a 16 MMAs) | 475 | 99% |
| A and B re-read from LDS (the GEMM's 8 a 16 MMAs, 32 `ds_load_b64`) | 467 | 97% |
| the LDS reads **and** the barrier | 438 | 91% |
| the reads as 16-lane exchanges (`XCHG`: half the LDS bytes, +12 VALU a fragment) | 397 | 83% |
| the exchange and the barrier | 384 | 80% |

Four things it settles. **VALU issue is not free beside the MMAs**: four
FMAs per MMA cost 12%, which is 4 clocks of a 34-clock wave32 MMA, and it
stays linear to 8 a MMA (dual-issue softens 16). So the 16-MMA tile's
budget for everything that is not an MMA is a few instructions, and the
shipped kernel was spending ~50. **The LDS bandwidth is not the limit**:
the GEMM's own read pattern costs 3% (G-o8's "LDS rate for replicated
reads" candidate is dead), and a barrier alone costs nothing. **The two
together cost 9%**: the burst of every wave's reads after the barrier,
which is the lockstep candidate, and which is confirmed on the real kernel
below. And **halving the LDS bytes with `v_permlanex16` loses**: the
exchange is 4 permutes and 8 selects a fragment (ACO lowers
`subgroupShuffleXor(v, 16)` at wave32 to `v_permlanex16_b32`, a VALU op
with no LDS traffic, and the coopmat is assembled from the dwords with no
sub-dword moves), 96 VALU a tile, ~14% of the pipe for a 3% saving.

**The real kernel** (`H3_SHAPES=480 H3_PROFILE=1 H3_BANK=q8`, int8, the
machine otherwise idle, 100 ms clock and package samples; per clock is
FLOP/clk/CU against 480 at the sampled clock; every arm through
`H3_GEMM_SPV` + `H3_GEMM_KRANGE_SPV`, the bit-identical ones through
`H3_GEMM_REF` against the shipped build's velocities):

| build | qkv | gate / up | o | down | forward | sclk | W | per clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| shipped `lds_w32` (§2.9; the K tiles unrolled) | 40.4 | 40.3 / 40.4 | 39.0 | 40.3 | 27.30 s | 2643 | 154 | 382, **79.6%** |
| `LDS_XCHG` at pitch 40 (bit-identical) | 38.2 | 37.7 / 37.6 | 36.7 | 37.4 | 28.65 | 2653 | 152 | 360, 75% |
| `LDS_NOBAR`: no slab barrier (wrong by construction) | 49.5 | 49.8 / 49.8 | 49.4 | 48.6 | 23.52 | **2899** | **137** | 427, **89%** |
| `LDS_HALF_READS`: one tile's fragments for both (wrong) | 43.1 | 43.1 / 42.9 | 42.2 | 42.2 | 26.56 | 2683 | 153 | 402, 84% |
| **`KT_LOOP` + `STAGE_RW`** (bit-identical; **shipped**) | **43.5** | **43.2 / 42.9** | **42.4** | **42.2** | **26.71** | 2672 | 153 | 407, **84.8%** |
| … + `LOAD_ORDER` (first MMA after 8 reads, not 20) | 42.9 | 43.0 / 42.8 | 42.1 | 41.9 | 26.48 | 2677 | 153 | 401, 83.5% |
| … as a four-wave 128×128 workgroup (three a WGP) | 38.8 | 38.4 / 38.2 | 36.9 | 39.1 | 28.08 | 2726 | 152 | 356, 74% |

**How the moves arise, from the disassembly** (`RADV_DEBUG=asm`,
`cmd/probe`, wave32). The shipped slab body issues its six staging
`buffer_load_b128`, then 40 `ds_load_b64` (the first tile's eight
fragments and the second's first two), a `lgkmcnt` ladder with four MMAs
a rung, then the second tile's remaining 24 reads — and in the middle of
it the *next* slab's six staging loads, hoisted across the barrier
(`barrier()` orders shared memory only; a read-only buffer load may move
through it). At 256 VGPRs with 128 of accumulators, 64 of first-tile
fragments and 24 of staging registers there is no contiguous room for the
second tile's 64, so its reads land in the address registers' free pairs
(`v[10:11]`, `v[24:25]`, `v[1:2]`, …) and are `v_swap_b32`'d into
8-register operands behind `s_waitcnt lgkmcnt(N)` steps: 16 swaps and 16
dual moves in one unrolled body, 30 in the other, plus ~17 address ops.
With the tiles as a loop, each iteration is 32 `ds_load_b64`, 2 VALU, 4
waitcnts, 16 MMAs and a branch; the slab's wrapper is the six loads, ~15
address ops and the six `ds_store_2addr_b64`. Two compiler facts on the
way: **NIR sinks a read-only SSBO load to its use** (with the loop in
between, the staging loads went to just before the stores, latency fully
exposed — `nir_opt_access` infers `readonly` back from the absence of a
store, so `STAGE_RW` also plants a never-taken store to each view); and a
buffer-semantics fence on the barrier (`LDS_FENCE`) does not stop the
hoist and changes no instruction.

**What is left, priced.** After this build the gap is ~15 points, and the
arms bound each part: the barrier's lockstep **≤ 9** (`LDS_NOBAR`, an
upper bound: the race also frees the LDS and the non-finite data drops
the power, hence its 2899 MHz), the LDS reads **~4** (`LDS_HALF_READS`
gains 4 with half of them), the global side **~3** (§2.9's `STAGE_L0`).
The exchange cannot buy the 4 (it costs 14 to save 3); a bigger wave tile
cannot (4×8 at wave32 is 256 VGPRs of accumulators); a 128×128 workgroup
that fits three a WGP loses 11% to the global side before its barrier
saving can show; and the LDS geometry admits no third tile a slab
(three-tile planes at any conflict-free pitch are 72–80 KB
double-buffered against a 64 KB workgroup limit). So the remaining lever
is the barrier itself: a slab structure that lets the two workgroups on a
WGP, or the eight waves of one, stay out of phase.

**The rule this adds** (to §2.9's three): on RDNA3.5 **count the VALU
instructions a tile the way the bytes were counted before** — a
`v_swap`, a `v_cndmask`, a `v_permlanex16` and an address add each cost
the matrix pipe a clock, ~3% for every instruction a MMA at wave32. Read
the disassembly for moves before timing a build, and prefer a loop the
compiler cannot reschedule over an unrolled body it will "improve".

**Reproduce.** The shipped build is the `go generate` line for
`dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32` (`-DKT_LOOP=1 -DSTAGE_RW=1` added; the
`_krange` companion likewise). The arms: `-DLDS_XCHG=1` (`A_LPITCH`/
`B_LPITCH` 40 or 36), `-DLDS_NOBAR=1`, `-DLDS_HALF_READS=1`,
`-DLOAD_ORDER=1`, `-DLDS_FENCE=1`, `-DWAVES_M=2 -DWAVES_N=2` on
`dit_gemm.comp`, compiled to the scratchpad and screened as §2.9 says
(`H3_GEMM_BM`/`H3_GEMM_BN` pin a workgroup tile other than 128×256). The
probe: the `wmma_issue_*` generate lines in `shaders/shaders.go`, run
with `PEAK_SPV=<list> PEAK_MMAS=16 PEAK_SUBGROUPS=8 PEAK_WAVE=32 go run
./cmd/bench peak` (`results/peak.csv` holds the rows).

| added to the register-only loop | FLOP/clk/CU | of 480 |
|---|---|---|
| nothing (`wmma_issue_reg`) | 480–491 | 100% |
| 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 independent fp32 FMAs a lane per MMA | 449 / 422 / 382 / 318 | 93.5 / 88 / 80 / 66% |
| a workgroup barrier every 16 MMAs | 480 | 100% |
| the A fragments re-read from LDS each tile (4 a 16 MMAs) | 475 | 99% |
| A and B re-read from LDS (the GEMM's 8 a 16 MMAs, 32 `ds_load_b64`) | 467 | 97% |
| the LDS reads **and** the barrier | 438 | 91% |
| the reads as 16-lane exchanges (`XCHG`: half the LDS bytes, +12 VALU a fragment) | 397 | 83% |
| the exchange and the barrier | 384 | 80% |

FMAs per MMA cost 12%, which is 4 clocks of a 34-clock wave32 MMA, and it
stays linear to 8 a MMA (dual-issue softens 16). So the 16-MMA tile's
budget for everything that is not an MMA is a few instructions, and the
shipped kernel was spending ~50. **The LDS bandwidth is not the limit**:
the GEMM's own read pattern costs 3% (G-o8's "LDS rate for replicated
reads" candidate is dead), and a barrier alone costs nothing. **The two
together cost 9%**: the burst of every wave's reads after the barrier,
which is the lockstep candidate, and which is confirmed on the real kernel
below. And **halving the LDS bytes with `v_permlanex16` loses**: the
exchange is 4 permutes and 8 selects a fragment (ACO lowers
`subgroupShuffleXor(v, 16)` at wave32 to `v_permlanex16_b32`, a VALU op
with no LDS traffic, and the coopmat is assembled from the dwords with no
sub-dword moves), 96 VALU a tile, ~14% of the pipe for a 3% saving.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| shipped `lds_w32` (§2.9; the K tiles unrolled) | 40.4 | 40.3 / 40.4 | 39.0 | 40.3 | 27.30 s | 2643 | 154 | 382, **79.6%** |

| `LDS_HALF_READS`: one tile's fragments for both (wrong) | 43.1 | 43.1 / 42.9 | 42.2 | 42.2 | 26.56 | 2683 | 153 | 402, 84% |

fragments and the second's first two), a `lgkmcnt` ladder with four MMAs
a rung, then the second tile's remaining 24 reads — and in the middle of

through it). At 256 VGPRs with 128 of accumulators, 64 of first-tile
fragments and 24 of staging registers there is no contiguous room for the
second tile's 64, so its reads land in the address registers' free pairs

8-register operands behind `s_waitcnt lgkmcnt(N)` steps: 16 swaps and 16
dual moves in one unrolled body, 30 in the other, plus ~17 address ops.

waitcnts, 16 MMAs and a branch; the slab's wrapper is the six loads, ~15
address ops and the six `ds_store_2addr_b64`. Two compiler facts on the
way: **NIR sinks a read-only SSBO load to its use** (with the loop in
between, the staging loads went to just before the stores, latency fully
exposed — `nir_opt_access` infers `readonly` back from the absence of a
store, so `STAGE_RW` also plants a never-taken store to each view); and a
buffer-semantics fence on the barrier (`LDS_FENCE`) does not stop the
hoist and changes no instruction.

arms bound each part: the barrier's lockstep **≤ 9** (`LDS_NOBAR`, an
upper bound: the race also frees the LDS and the non-finite data drops
the power, hence its 2899 MHz), the LDS reads **~4** (`LDS_HALF_READS`
gains 4 with half of them), the global side **~3** (§2.9's `STAGE_L0`).

cannot (4×8 at wave32 is 256 VGPRs of accumulators); a 128×128 workgroup
that fits three a WGP loses 11% to the global side before its barrier
saving can show; and the LDS geometry admits no third tile a slab
(three-tile planes at any conflict-free pitch are 72–80 KB
double-buffered against a 64 KB workgroup limit). So the remaining lever
is the barrier itself: a slab structure that lets the two workgroups on a
WGP, or the eight waves of one, stay out of phase.

instructions a tile the way the bytes were counted before** — a
`v_swap`, a `v_cndmask`, a `v_permlanex16` and an address add each cost
the matrix pipe a clock, ~3% for every instruction a MMA at wave32. Read
the disassembly for moves before timing a build, and prefer a loop the
compiler cannot reschedule over an unrolled body it will "improve".

probe: the `wmma_issue_*` generate lines in `shaders/shaders.go`, run
with `PEAK_SPV=<list> PEAK_MMAS=16 PEAK_SUBGROUPS=8 PEAK_WAVE=32 go run
./cmd/bench peak` (`results/peak.csv` holds the rows).

content.text:
G-o8 is answered and the GEMM ships one step faster, bit-identical, with every host's gate passing.

**What the next item was.** KERNELS.md's handoff named G-o8 first: the shipped LDS-staged wave32 GEMM sat at 80% of the ceiling per clock, and the record blamed the ~18 missing points on the LDS side (64 reads, 6 stores, a barrier per slab).

**What I found.** Most of it was none of those. I wrote a probe (`shaders/wmma_issue_probe.comp`, run through a new `PEAK_SPV` hook on `cmd/bench peak`) that adds the kernel's parts back to the register-only WMMA loop one at a time, in the GEMM's own geometry:

- Every VALU instruction beside an MMA costs the matrix pipe about one clock on this part. Four FMAs per MMA cost 12%, eight cost 20%.
- The GEMM's LDS reads cost 3%, a barrier alone nothing, the two together 9% (the post-barrier burst). LDS bandwidth is not a limit.
- The shipped build's disassembly carried about 40 register moves per K tile: the allocator assembling the second tile's fragments while hoisted staging loads held the registers. That was ~7% of the pipe.

**What shipped.** The slab's two K tiles kept as a loop the compiler may not unroll (`-DKT_LOOP=1 -DSTAGE_RW=1`, now in the `dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32` generate lines), same MMAs in the same order. Two runs on H3's 480p shapes:

| | qkv | gate / up | o | down | 480p forward | per clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| shipped before | 40.4 | 40.3 / 40.4 | 39.0 | 40.3 | 27.30 s | 80% |
| kt-loop, runs 1 / 2 | 43.5 / 42.8 | 43.2 / 42.7 | 42.4 / 41.9 | 42.2 / 41.9 | 26.71 / 26.54 s | 85% |

`TestGPUForward` is bit-identical, and the gates of all eight other hosts of the kernel pass unchanged. 

**Measured dead, so not to be re-run:** halving the LDS bytes with a 16-lane exchange (`v_permlanex16` is VALU: −5% despite being bit-identical), a finer load order (a wash), and a four-wave 128×128 workgroup (−11%, the global side). The no-barrier arm bounds what is left in the GEMM at ≤ 9 points, and the LDS geometry admits no deeper slab, so the remaining lever is a slab structure that keeps waves out of phase.

**Record:** `research/2.10-valu-costs-matrix-clocks.md`, its README row, KERNELS.md (G2b row, the ceiling table, G-o8 closed, a new G-o9, the session-5 handoff), VIDEO.md M11, TODO.md, the probe rows in `results/peak.csv`, and a memory note. Nothing is committed; the auto-committer owns main. The one thing to know for G4 and G5 next: count `v_swap`/`v_mov`/`v_cndmask` per MMA in the ISA before timing any build, because the budget is a few instructions an MMA.
